content: The overuse and misuse of antibiotics in both animals and humans are significantly contributing to the growing threat of antibiotic resistance. Certain bacteria that cause severe infections in humans have already developed resistance to most or all available treatments, and there are very few promising alternatives currently in development. If no action is taken, by 2050, nearly all existing antibiotics will become ineffective in preventing and treating human diseases, with the economic cost of losing these drugs exceeding $100 trillion in terms of global productivity. Scientific evidence has clearly demonstrated that the overuse of antibiotics in animals can lead to the emergence of antibiotic resistance. The World Health Organization (WHO) has issued guidelines to address this issue, building on decades of expert reports and evaluations regarding the role of agricultural antibiotic use in the increasing threat of resistance. These guidelines are a direct response to the WHO Global Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance adopted in 2015 and the political declaration from the United Nations General Assembly in 2016. They recognize the global nature of antibiotic resistance and the rapid spread of resistant organisms and genetic determinants across continents. Furthermore, they acknowledge that all uses of antibiotics, whether in humans or animals, contribute to the development of resistance in bacteria. The WHO guidelines emphasize the importance of controlling antibiotic use in food-producing animals to combat antimicrobial resistance worldwide. This is because antibiotics used in food animals are often identical or similar to those used in human medicine, and the volume of antibiotic use in animals, including for growth promotion, is increasing globally due to rising demand for animal proteins. Additionally, foodborne diseases, including bacterial infections, remain a major cause of illness and death, particularly in children. The prolonged use of multiple antibiotics at sub-therapeutic doses in food production is associated with the development of multi-drug-resistant pathogens. Humans are exposed to resistant bacteria originating from animal production through various pathways, including contaminated food, direct contact with animals, and environmental exposure. The WHO recommends a significant reduction in the use of all medically important antibiotics in food-producing animals. It also calls for a complete ban on the use of these antibiotics for growth promotion and disease prevention in the absence of diagnosed disease. Antibiotics classified as critically important for human medicine should not be used for controlling the spread of clinically diagnosed infectious diseases within groups of food-producing animals. Furthermore, antibiotics classified as highest priority critically important for human medicine should not be used for treating food-producing animals with clinically diagnosed infectious diseases unless no other treatment options are available, and only under the guidance of a qualified veterinarian. The guidelines also include best practice statements, such as ensuring that any new class of antibiotics developed for human use is considered critically important for human medicine unless otherwise categorized by WHO. Medically important antibiotics not currently used in food production should not be introduced for such purposes in the future. The recommendations were developed by a diverse group of experts from various fields, including human and veterinary medicine, microbiology, antimicrobial resistance, agricultural economics, and veterinary ethics. The process followed stringent WHO methodologies, including the use of the GRADE system to evaluate the reliability of evidence. Systematic reviews assessed the associations between antibiotic use in food-producing animals and the risks of human exposure to drug-resistant pathogens, while narrative reviews evaluated the transfer of resistance determinants from animals to humans and the unintended consequences of restricting antibiotic use in agriculture. Implementing these guidelines may require significant changes in current practices in food animal production. Alternatives to antibiotics, such as improved hygiene, enhanced biosecurity, and better use of vaccines, have been shown to be effective in maintaining productivity and animal health without relying on antibiotics for growth promotion or disease prevention. Countries that have already prohibited the use of antimicrobial growth promoters can provide valuable insights for implementation, particularly in developing regions. International support for technical resources, microbiology, and drug-resistance testing, as well as increased veterinary expertise, is crucial for the successful implementation of these guidelines. Access to veterinary professionals is essential for making informed decisions about antibiotic use in treating and preventing disease in animal groups. WHO encourages countries to establish national surveillance programs to monitor antibiotic use in agriculture and the presence of resistance in food animals, consumer food products, human populations, and the environment using the integrated One Health approach. The WHO will evaluate the uptake of these guidelines through ongoing monitoring and evaluation efforts by Member States as part of the Global Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance. The guidelines will be reviewed and updated five years after publication, or earlier if significant new evidence emerges.
